name: side-effect-free-function
intent: Put the model's logic into operations that compute a result from their inputs alone, so that a caller - and a test - can predict the result without knowing any state the operation might secretly touch.
problem: Reasoning about a design becomes guesswork when operations do more than return a result: the caller must read the implementation and every delegation to know which state a call changes, and no result can be reproduced in a test without recreating the state around it. As rules compose, the number of hidden interactions grows faster than the behaviour being built, so the model stops being safely predictable.
context: Applies inside the model layer of any codebase whose rules are combined and composed - pricing, eligibility, allocation, validation - and where a computation must be exercised in tests without a database, clock or message broker in the loop. It matters most where several rules interact (composition multiplies hidden coupling) and in languages whose defaults are mutable objects, because there the discipline has to be stated rather than assumed.
benefits: Results depend only on inputs, so a call can be replaced by its value: reasoning, refactoring and verification become local to the operation instead of spanning the object graph.
Tests need no fixtures: inputs in, value out, with no database, clock, broker or filesystem to arrange or clean up.
Composition stops multiplying uncertainty - combining several rules stays predictable because no rule can alter what the next one sees.
Memoization, parallel execution and re-ordering become safe, since repeated calls with the same inputs yield the same value with no order-dependent effects.
Hidden state stops leaking into the model: dependencies surface as parameters or constructor arguments instead of being read from globals.
Concurrency hazards shrink to the value boundary: two side-effect-free functions cannot race with each other over shared mutable state.
tradeoffs: Copy-and-return allocates: every modification builds a new value, which is visible in hot loops and large object graphs - the price paid to keep reasoning local.
Purity is declared, not verified, in most languages: one read of a clock, config singleton, current locale or random source silently voids the guarantee while the function still looks pure.
Pushing logic into values and standalone functions scatters behaviour away from the object that owns the data, so navigation gets harder and small types proliferate.
The strict command half - commands return no domain information - pushes callers into read-after-write and opens a re-read window under concurrency; relaxing it must be a stated decision.
Frameworks whose lazy loading or dirty tracking hides writes behind property getters (ORMs, proxies) fight the query/command split, so strict adoption needs explicit opt-outs at those boundaries.
Outside the languages that type-check mutation, the split is enforced by naming and review convention only, so it decays under schedule pressure.

participants.responsibility: Computes and returns a result from its inputs; it may read immutable state but writes nothing observable - no field, no parameter, no global, no I/O.
A deliberately simple operation that changes observable state and returns no domain information; the only place mutations are allowed.
Immutable carrier of a result or of a rule's input; complex logic moved onto it stays pure because no operation on it can change it.
The caller the guarantee is for: it may substitute a call with its result and compose queries without tracking hidden state.

use_cases: Pricing and discount rules: unit prices, tax and rebates computed from immutable inputs, so the same basket always prices the same way.
Eligibility and specification checks: a rule expressed as a predicate over a value and reused in validation, selection and tests.
Money and quantity arithmetic: scaling, adding and rounding return new values instead of adjusting a running total in place.
Deriving test data and expected values from the same pure functions the model uses, instead of hand-copied golden values.
Query-side report assembly: projections, summaries and totals built by composing pure functions over already-loaded immutable data.
Memoizing an expensive domain computation, which is sound exactly because the function is referentially transparent.

Redux reducers: the store computes the next state by calling (previousState, action) => newState with no mutation, no clock, no randomness, so DevTools can replay a recorded action log and reproduce the exact state and useSelector can detect changes by reference comparison alone.

React function components: the official contract is that rendering must be a pure function of props, state and context, so React can cache components whose inputs are unchanged, abandon an outdated render mid-flight, and call each component twice in Strict Mode to expose impurity.

Haskell: ordinary functions are pure by default and effects are confined to IO-typed values, so the type signature itself states whether a computation touches the world and the compiler, not review, enforces the query half of the split.
avoid_when: The operation is inherently an effect - sending mail, writing files, publishing a message - and cannot be modelled as a value: keep it a command at the edge instead.
The data is huge and the copy dominates the work: keep the loop in place behind a clearly named command and record the exception.
You want to cache before you have a pure function - memoizing a computation that reads time, randomness or I/O returns stale or wrong results.
A framework owns the object lifecycle (lazy loading, dirty tracking, proxies): its getters are effects by design, and pretending otherwise buys nothing.
The split cannot be enforced in review: queries with occasional hidden writes are worse than an honestly mutable design.
anti_patterns: "Getter with a side effect": a query that lazily initialises, logs, caches in a field or touches the database, so callers cannot reason about what reading it does.
"Update and return": a command that returns domain information, inviting callers to chain further decisions onto the state it just changed.
A "pure" function that mutates its arguments or a shared value object - sorting a parameter in place, appending to a collection field.
Reading ambient state inside a core computation (clock, locale, environment, randomness) and calling it pure because no parameter mentions the dependency.
Caching or parallelising an impure computation because the surrounding code is nominally functional.
design_principles: Command-query separation: a method either changes observable state or returns a result, never both.
Referential transparency: an expression can be replaced by its value without changing the program.
Immutability as the supporting structure: side effects are controlled by moving complex logic into value objects.
Information hiding: the dependencies a computation needs are made explicit as inputs instead of being read from hidden state.
Separation of concerns: model decisions stay free of I/O, persistence and framework lifecycle.
best_practices: Make the result the only output: return a new value instead of writing into a parameter, a field or a global.
Keep commands tiny and obvious: one observable change, no domain-shaped return value, a name that says what changed.
Move complex rules onto immutable values so the query side stays pure while the model grows.
Pass dependencies in - clock, configuration, identifiers, randomness - rather than reading them inside the computation.
Memoize only demonstrably pure functions with hashable keys, and bound the cache.
Test queries without fixtures: if a test needs a database, clock or broker to check a model rule, the rule is not a query yet.
Where copy-avoidance forces an in-place operation, keep it behind a narrow API and document that the query form still exists.
sources: Evans, E., Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software (2003) - Chapter 10 'Supple Design', pattern 'Side-Effect-Free Functions'.
